newsitem.title: INDONESIA: S.E.Asian Cocoa - Prices mixed, London seen up.
newsitem.headline: S.E.Asian Cocoa - Prices mixed, London seen up.

text.p: Southeast Asian cocoa prices were mixed on Wednesday, with Indonesian values gaining ground on active buying while Malaysian levels waned, traders said.
Indonesian traders said supply was rising steadily as the main crop harvest proceeded while demand outstripped supply in Malaysia, where players were resorting to imports.
"There are about 300 tonnes coming daily to Ujung Pandang," one Indonesian trader from the capital of the key growing region of South Sulawesi said by telephone.
"I expect arrivals to range between 600 and 700 tonnes daily during the peak of the harvest later this month," he said.
Traders said cocoa prices had risen to 2,950-2,975 rupiah/kg in Ujung Pandang from 2,800-2,850 rupiah/kg a week ago.

They said some exporters were short-covering to fill contracts, but others who had build up stocks during a buying spree when prices on the New York and London terminal markets were climbing were selling the beans back into the market.
"Some players who had bought aggressively when prices were high seemed to have run out of steam and are now selling the beans at lower prices," one trader said.
"I don't know why they are doing it," he said. "Maybe their purchases were based on emotions rather than strategies."
Another trader said he expected London July coffee futures to open higher by five to six pounds sterling later on Wednesday.

Late buying helped London cocoa prices erase earlier losses on Tuesday, with July ending up three pounds at 1,024 pounds. In New York, the benchmark July contract rose $9 a tonne to close at $1,449, after trading between $1,432 to $1,456.
Indonesian traders said 4,000 tonnes of cocoa beans were shipped to Brazil last week, and that the market was optimistic that the country would import more.
Brazilian producers had approved up to 15,000 tonnes of imports until August to make up for a shortfall at the start of the Bahian midcrop.
In Malaysia, players said they were still sourcing beans from overseas as local supply could not match demand.

"We can never have enough of local beans," said the trading manager at a local confectionery firm. "I'm still having to buy from Indonesia, Ivory Coast and other bases where price and trading terms aren't always right."
Traders said local consumers were reasonably covered for now and some were already buying for next year.
"At the moment, I'm already selling for April 1998," said one trader.

On Wednesday, the Malaysian Cocoa Board quoted Standard Malaysian Cocoa (SMC) Grade 1 A out of Tawau, the country's main growing area, at an average of 3,375 ringgit a tonne, down 45 ringgit from the week before.
The board quoted the SMC 1B grade out of Tawau at an average of 3,325 ringgit, also down 45 ringgit from previously.
Traders offered the SMC 1A at 3,325 ringgit a tonne and the SMC IB at between 3,400-3,410 ringgit.
(US$1=2,420 rupiah)
